title: A Random Matrix Theory of Masked Self-Supervised Learning
claim: Estimator error follows a sharp interpolation-type peak at a critical sample size, and stronger data correlation substantially lowers error.
layout: 2 vertically stacked line plots, shared x-axis, legend on top, dashed baselines
description: Two vertically stacked line plots share an x-axis, the sample size n from 0 to 800. A legend across the top lists three solid curves for rho = 0 (purple), 0.5 (pink-red) and 0.9 (yellow), plus a dashed purple line labeled App. Error. The top panel shows generalization error L(A-hat). Each curve spikes sharply near n = 200, which is the dimension d. The rho = 0 and rho = 0.5 curves diverge there and then decay slowly. The rho = 0.9 curve only has a small bump. Dashed horizontal lines mark the approximation error for each rho and carry labels at the right edge. The bottom panel shows training error. It is zero until n = 200, then rises and saturates, highest for rho = 0. Star markers for the empirical values sit on the solid theory curves. Grid lines run behind the curves.
caption: Generalization and Training Error for the SSR estimator for Gaussian data with a Toeplitz covariance $\Sigma_{i,j} = \rho^{|i-j|}$, for different values of $\rho$. The value $\rho=0$ corresponds to $\Sigma=I_d$. Solid lines correspond to the asymptotic limit, while dots correspond to the empirical error. In all curves, $d = 200$ and $\lambda = 10^{-4}$.
abstract: In the era of transformer models, masked self-supervised learning (SSL) has become a foundational training paradigm. A defining feature of masked SSL is that training aggregates predictions across many masking patterns, giving rise to a joint, matrix-valued predictor rather than a single vector-valued estimator. This object encodes how coordinates condition on one another and poses new analytical challenges. We develop a precise high-dimensional analysis of masked modeling objectives in the proportional regime where the number of samples scales with the ambient dimension. Our results provide explicit expressions for the generalization error and characterize the spectral structure of the learned predictor, revealing how masked modeling extracts structure from data. For spiked covariance models, we show that the joint predictor undergoes a Baik–Ben Arous–Péché (BBP)-type phase transition, identifying when masked SSL begins to recover latent signals. Finally, we identify structured regimes in which masked self-supervised learning provably outperforms PCA, highlighting potential advantages of SSL objectives over classical unsupervised methods.
